title: Inequalities in real-world situations
blurb: Translate limits and minimums into inequalities, solve them (flipping the sign when you must) and interpret the answer in context.
question: A patient may drink no more than 1,500 mL of fluid a day. He has already had 900 mL, and each cup holds 240 mL. The TEAS asks for the greatest number of full cups he may still drink. How do you write, solve and interpret the inequality?

teach.h: A limit, not a single answer
teach.body: Formally, an inequality is a statement that compares two expressions using <, >, ≤ or ≥, and its solution is a whole set of values rather than one number. In plain English: an equation says 'exactly this much'; an inequality says 'no more than' or 'at least'. Budgets, fluid limits, minimum hours and maximum doses are all inequalities, and the TEAS tests whether you can write one, solve it and make sense of the answer.

rows: at least, no less than, minimum

teach.h: Solve like an equation, with one exception
teach.body: Add, subtract, multiply and divide on both sides exactly as you would for an equation. The one new rule: when you multiply or divide both sides by a NEGATIVE number, reverse the inequality sign. Example: −3x > 12. Divide by −3 and flip: x < −4. Test it: x = −5 gives −3(−5) = 15, and 15 > 12 is true. x = 0 gives 0, and 0 > 12 is false. So the solutions really are below −4.

rows.label: Check by
values: Testing a value in the range

teach.text: Two opposite slips. Forgetting to flip when dividing by a negative (−3x > 12 written as x > −4), and flipping when the divisor is positive but the answer is negative (4x > −12 is x > −3, no flip). Only the sign of the number you multiply or divide by matters. And 'at least' is ≥, not >; 'no more than' is ≤, not <.

teach.h: Graphing c ≤ 2.5 on a number line
teach.caption: Closed (filled) circle for ≤ or ≥; open circle for < or >. Shade toward the solutions.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr. Alvarez's fluid limit
items: Limit: no more than 1,500 mL a day. Already taken: 900 mL. Cups: 240 mL each. Let c = cups still allowed.
Divide by 240 (positive, so no flip): c ≤ 2.5. Check: 240 × 2.5 = 600. ✓
Interpret: only FULL cups count, and 3 cups (720 mL) would break the limit. Answer: 2 cups.

teach.h: Rounding a decimal answer in context
teach.caption: Ignore the usual 'round 5 up' rule here: the limit decides the direction.

teach.h: Worked examples: a minimum, and a negative coefficient
items: Tasha, a nursing assistant, earns $16 an hour and needs at least $500 this week. 16h ≥ 500, so h ≥ 31.25.
Check: 16 × 31.25 = 500. ✓ With whole hours, 31 hours pays only $496, so she must work at least 32 hours.
Solve 5 − 2x ≥ 11. Subtract 5: −2x ≥ 6. Divide by −2 and FLIP: x ≤ −3.
Test x = −4: 5 − 2(−4) = 13, and 13 ≥ 11. ✓ Test x = 0: 5 ≥ 11 is false, so 0 is correctly excluded.
Compound inequalities such as 3 < x ≤ 8 mean x is greater than 3 AND at most 8.
At least / minimum = ≥. At most / no more than / maximum = ≤.
Solve like an equation, but flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Closed circle for ≤ and ≥; open circle for < and >.
Interpret the answer: round down for 'at most' whole items, round up for 'at least'.
Test one value from your answer in the original inequality.

summary: You can now translate phrases like 'at least' and 'no more than' into inequality symbols, solve inequalities (flipping the sign only for a negative multiplier or divisor) and graph them. You can also turn a decimal answer into the right whole number for the real-world limit.

A.q: A nursing scholarship requires a GPA of no less than 3.2. Which inequality describes an eligible GPA, g?
A.why: 'No less than 3.2' means 3.2 or anything above it, so 3.2 itself counts: g ≥ 3.2.

whyNot.0: g > 3.2 leaves out a GPA of exactly 3.2, which is 'no less than 3.2'.
whyNot.1: g ≤ 3.2 describes a maximum; 'no less than' sets a minimum.
whyNot.3: g < 3.2 describes the GPAs that do NOT qualify.

A.why: Subtract 7: −4x > 24. Divide by −4 and flip the sign: x < −6. Test x = −7: 28 + 7 = 35 > 31. ✓

whyNot.0: Dividing by −4 requires flipping the sign; x > −6 keeps it unflipped.
whyNot.2: x > 6 loses the negative and does not flip the sign.
whyNot.3: x < 6 flips the sign but loses the negative: 24 ÷ (−4) = −6.

A.q: Which description matches the number-line graph of x ≤ −2?
A.why: ≤ includes −2, so the circle is closed (filled). 'Less than' values lie to the left on a number line.

whyNot.1: An open circle excludes −2; that graph shows x < −2.
whyNot.2: Shading right shows values greater than −2: x ≥ −2.
whyNot.3: An open circle shaded right shows x > −2.

B.q: A patient may drink no more than 2,000 mL per day. By 3 p.m. she has had 1,280 mL. Each glass holds 200 mL. What is the greatest number of FULL glasses she may still drink today?
B.why: 1,280 + 200g ≤ 2,000, so 200g ≤ 720 and g ≤ 3.6. Only full glasses count, and 4 glasses (800 mL) would exceed the limit, so the answer is 3.

whyNot.1: 4 rounds 3.6 up. Four glasses add 800 mL, giving 2,080 mL, which breaks the limit.
whyNot.2: 6 divides the amount already taken (1,280 ÷ 200 = 6.4) instead of the amount left.
whyNot.3: 10 divides the whole daily limit by 200 and ignores the 1,280 mL already taken.

B.q: Jordan earns $17.50 per hour plus a $45 weekly stipend and wants to earn at least $600 this week. What is the minimum number of whole hours he must work?

whyNot.0: 31 rounds down: 17.50 × 31 + 45 = 587.50, which is short of $600.
whyNot.3: 37 adds the stipend instead of subtracting it: 645 ÷ 17.50 = 36.86, rounded up.

B.q: Which value of x is a solution of 3x − 5 ≤ 2x + 1?
B.why: Subtract 2x: x − 5 ≤ 1. Add 5: x ≤ 6. The sign ≤ includes 6. Check: 3(6) − 5 = 13 and 2(6) + 1 = 13, and 13 ≤ 13. ✓

C.why: Distribute: −2x + 6 ≥ 14. Subtract 6: −2x ≥ 8. Divide by −2 and flip: x ≤ −4. Test x = −5: −2(−8) = 16 ≥ 14. ✓

whyNot.0: x ≥ −4 forgets to flip the sign after dividing by −2.
whyNot.1: x ≤ −10 distributes −2 × −3 as −6 instead of +6, giving −2x ≥ 20.
whyNot.2: x ≥ 4 drops the negative and does not flip the sign.

C.q: Lena has $85 to spend on uniforms. She must buy one pair of pants for $24, and tops cost $18 each. What is the greatest number of tops she can buy?
C.why: 24 + 18t ≤ 85, so 18t ≤ 61 and t ≤ 3.39. Only whole tops, and 4 tops would cost 24 + 72 = $96. Answer: 3.

whyNot.0: 2 divides the money left by the price of the pants (61 ÷ 24) instead of by the price of a top.
whyNot.2: 4 rounds 3.39 up (or ignores the pants: 85 ÷ 18 = 4.7). Four tops plus pants cost $96.
whyNot.3: 6 adds the $24 instead of subtracting it: 109 ÷ 18 = 6.06.

C.why: Multiplying both sides of x/(−3) < 2 by −3 requires a flip: x > −6. Test x = 0: 0 < 2. ✓

whyNot.0: Dividing by −5 flips the sign: −5x ≤ 20 gives x ≥ −4.
whyNot.1: Dividing by positive 4 keeps the sign, even though the result is negative: x > −3.
whyNot.2: Adding 6 never flips the sign: x − 6 ≥ −2 gives x ≥ 4.

reteach.title: A height bar at a parking garage
reteach.question: A garage sign says 'Maximum clearance 7 ft'. A theme park ride says 'Riders must be at least 48 in tall'. How are these signs inequalities, and what does each one let through?

blocks.body: 'Maximum clearance 7 ft' means a vehicle's height v must be 7 ft or less: v ≤ 7. A van exactly 7 ft tall fits, so the circle is closed. 'At least 48 in' means a rider's height r is 48 in or more: r ≥ 48. Flipping the sign when dividing by a negative is like looking at the same sign in a mirror: everything reverses, including which way the arrow points.

blocks.text: 'Maximum' and 'at most' set a ceiling (≤); 'minimum' and 'at least' set a floor (≥). Both include the boundary value itself.

explain.body: At least, no less than, minimum: ≥. At most, no more than, maximum, does not exceed: ≤. More than or exceeds: >. Less than, fewer than or below: <.

test.q: A daily dose d must not exceed 4 grams. Which inequality describes d?
test.why: 'Must not exceed 4' allows 4 grams or less, so d ≤ 4.

whyNot.0: d < 4 leaves out exactly 4 grams, which does not exceed the limit.
whyNot.1: d ≥ 4 sets a minimum; the stem sets a maximum.
whyNot.3: d > 4 describes doses that break the limit.

explain.body: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Adding or subtracting never flips it, and dividing by a positive never flips it.

test.why: Subtract 9: −3x < 12. Divide by −3 and flip: x > −4. Test x = 0: 9 < 21. ✓

whyNot.0: x < −4 forgets to flip the sign when dividing by −3.
whyNot.2: x > 4 flips the sign but loses the negative: 12 ÷ (−3) = −4.
whyNot.3: x < 4 neither flips the sign nor keeps the negative.

explain.body: Closed (filled) circle when the boundary is included (≤, ≥); open circle when it is not (<, >). Shade right for greater than, left for less than.

test.q: On a number line, how is the solution x > 3 shown?
test.why: > does not include 3, so the circle is open, and greater values lie to the right.

whyNot.1: A closed circle includes 3; that graph shows x ≥ 3.
whyNot.2: Shading left shows values less than 3: x < 3.
whyNot.3: A closed circle shaded left shows x ≤ 3.

explain.body: A decimal answer often has to become a whole number. For a minimum ('at least'), round UP so you have enough. For a maximum ('at most'), round DOWN so you stay under the limit.

test.q: Gloves come in boxes of 50. A hospital unit needs at least 1,180 gloves. What is the least number of boxes it must order?
test.why: 50b ≥ 1,180, so b ≥ 23.6. Boxes are whole and this is a minimum, so round up: 24 boxes (1,200 gloves).

whyNot.0: 23 boxes hold 1,150 gloves, short of the 1,180 needed.
whyNot.1: 23.6 is not a whole number of boxes; the answer must be interpreted in context.
